# Surface and Geometry Alignment

Also called: Surface-aligned Gaussian Optimization, Geometry-guided Gaussian Splatting

## Overview
This family of methods aligns the discrete 3D Gaussian representation with continuous geometric priors to enforce surface consistency, addressing the ambiguity of semi-transparent primitives in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike standard photometric optimization which may produce floating artifacts, these methods introduce geometric loss terms to ensure Gaussian centers lie on the scene surface and their orientations align with surface normals [S1]. This enables the extraction of watertight meshes or physically-based inverse rendering, distinguishing it from pure appearance-based optimization [S1].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the goal of aligning the discrete Gaussian representation with a continuous geometric prior. The core mechanism involves adding geometric loss terms to the standard photometric rendering loss $\mathcal{L}_{rgb}$. These losses typically enforce two properties:
1.  **Positional Consistency:** Gaussian centers $\mathbf{c}_i$ are encouraged to lie on the zero-level set of a distance function (SDF or UDF) or align with metric depth estimates.
2.  **Normal Consistency:** The orientation of the Gaussians (derived from their covariance matrix or rotation quaternion) is aligned with the surface normal estimated from the geometric prior.

The total loss function generally takes the form:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{total} = \mathcal{L}_{rgb} + \lambda_{geo} \mathcal{L}_{geo} + \lambda_{norm} \mathcal{L}_{norm} $$
where $\mathcal{L}_{geo}$ is the geometric consistency loss and $\mathcal{L}_{norm}$ is the normal consistency loss [S1]. The weights $\lambda_{geo}$ and $\lambda_{norm}$ are hyperparameters that balance photometric fidelity against geometric accuracy [S1].

## Subtopics

### [SuGaR](9191-sugar.md)
SuGaR is a post-hoc method that extracts watertight 3D surfaces from a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model by introducing a self-regularization loss to align Gaussian primitives with the underlying scene geometry. It distinguishes itself from implicit surface methods by enforcing alignment through a penalty term that minimizes the distance between the camera and the closest Gaussian relative to rendered depth, followed by Poisson mesh reconstruction. While it enables mesh extraction from 3DGS, it is noted that current discrete geometry methods based on 3DGS may achieve comparable or worse results compared to continuous implicit representations.

### [Geo-Splatting](9201-geo-splatting.md)
Geo-Splatting is a physically-based inverse rendering method that augments 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with explicit geometric priors to improve normal estimation and light transport modeling. It solves the problem of noisy material decomposition and flawed relighting inherent in existing 3DGS-based methods that rely on approximated Gaussian normals. Unlike siblings that use implicit constraints or low-frequency spherical Gaussians, Geo-Splatting differentiably constructs surface-aligned Gaussian points from an optimizable explicit mesh, leveraging well-defined mesh normals and opaque surfaces for accurate self-occlusion and reflective surface handling.

### Surface-guided Gaussian Re-initialization
A method that proposes a surface-guided Gaussians re-initialization strategy to make the trained Gaussians better fit the input monocular video [S1]. It resolves the unbalanced aggregation of Gaussians caused by densification and splitting operations [S1].

## Background
The concept of aligning Gaussian primitives with geometric surfaces emerged as a solution to the "floating artifact" problem in 3DGS, where semi-transparent Gaussians do not strictly represent surfaces. Early works like SplattingAvatar and GoMAvatar embedded Gaussians onto canonical human body meshes using barycentric coordinates and normal displacements [S1]. Subsequent research, such as GVA, introduced re-initialization strategies to correct aggregation imbalances [S1]. The field has since diverged into post-hoc surface extraction (SuGaR) and explicit mesh-guided inverse rendering (Geo-Splatting), driven by the need for watertight meshes and physically accurate material decomposition [S1].
